Chapter 7: The Myths We Tell Ourselves—Challenging False Narratives
Living with depression isn’t just about facing the illness itself. It’s also about confronting the stories we tell ourselves about what it means to struggle. And let’s be honest, society is filled with myths about mental health. These ideas? They don’t just make recovery harder—they can also deepen that feeling of being all alone.
For a long time, there was this young man who thought happiness was something everyone else had already figured out. Maybe you’ve felt that way, too. He believed that if he just tried harder, he could simply “snap out of it.” He worried his pain made him weak, or that he was somehow broken. Even though he rarely said these things out loud, those beliefs quietly shaped how he saw himself—and what his future might look like.
Everything started to change when he began opening up, connecting with people from all walks of life who had their own struggles. Imagine his surprise when a colleague, always cheerful on the outside, admitted to feeling lost and anxious. Or when an old friend, admired for her confidence, confessed she’d battled depression for years. The more stories he heard, the clearer it became: suffering is just part of being human.
One evening, over dinner with friends, the topic of mental health came up. Someone joked, “Just think positive!” For a moment, that old shame crept back in. But then, another friend gently pushed back, challenging the idea that willpower alone could cure depression. The table went quiet, and in that silence, something shifted. It was suddenly obvious—the myths we carry can be more damaging than the illness itself.
It’s easy to fall into the trap of comparing your insides to everyone else’s outsides, isn’t it? Social media, with its endless parade of perfect moments, can make it seem like everyone else is thriving. But behind those smiles and successes, most people are carrying burdens of their own.
Challenging these false beliefs—it’s not a one-time thing. It’s a process. It means questioning the idea that suffering is some kind of personal failure. It means realizing that asking for help isn’t a sign of weakness. Mental illness isn’t a character flaw. It’s part of life, and it deserves both understanding and care.
Over time, the young man learned to show himself a little more kindness. He stopped measuring his worth by how productive he was, or by how well he could “hold it all together.” He began to realize that vulnerability isn’t something to hide—it’s actually a source of strength.
The stories we tell ourselves? They matter. Change those stories, and you just might change everything.
